6.SP-1#0: The mean is the total of the values shared equally among them.
Add the three values to get the total: 10 + 20 + 30 = 60.
There are 3 values, so divide the total by 3: 60 ÷ 3 = 20.
The mean of the three numbers is 20.
6.SP-1#1: The median is the middle value once the numbers are in order.
Sort the numbers from least to greatest: 2, 4, 5, 8, 9.
There are 5 values, so the middle one is the 3rd.
The 3rd value is 5, so the median is 5.
6.SP-2#0: Check for a value that is far from the others, because it affects the mean more than the median.
200 is an outlier: the mean is (30 + 32 + 35 + 200) ÷ 4 = 74.25, far above three of the four salaries.
The median is halfway between 32 and 35, which is 33.5, close to most salaries.
The median is the better choice for a typical salary.
6.SP-2#1: The median is the middle value of the sorted list.
The list 4, 4, 10 is already in order and has 3 values.
The middle (2nd) value is 4, so the median is 4.
6.SP-3#0: The range is the largest value minus the smallest value.
Find the extremes: the max is 22 and the min is 6.
Subtract the min from the max: 22 − 6 = 16, so the range is 16.
6.SP-3#1: The range measures how far the data stretches from min to max.
Every value is 7, so the max is 7 and the min is 7.
Subtract the min from the max: 7 − 7 = 0, so the range is 0.
6.SP-4#0: On a dot plot, each dot stands for one data point.
The dots above 2 are the data points that equal 2.
There are 4 dots there, so 4 data points are 2.
6.SP-4#1: Think about which display is built from the five-number summary.
A bar graph only compares counts for separate categories.
A box plot marks the quartiles with the box edges and the median with a line inside.
The answer is the box plot.
6.SP-5#0: Think of the word for a value that lies outside the main group.
Most data values sit close together, but this one is far away from all of them.
Such a value is called an outlier.
6.SP-5#1: Center tells only what a typical value is.
A good description also says how spread out the values are, using range or IQR.
It can also mention shape, such as skew, clusters or gaps.
One good answer is spread (shape also works).
6.SP-6#0: The mode is the value that appears most often.
Count each value: 6 appears three times, while 2 and 9 appear once each.
6 appears the most, so the mode is 6.
6.SP-6#1: Each number in the list is one data point.
Count the numbers one by one: 11, 13, 15, 17.
That is four numbers, so there are 4 data points.
6.SP-7#0: A statistical question expects answers that vary.
This one asks about each student, and students take different amounts of time to eat.
The answers will vary, so yes, it is statistical.
6.SP-7#1: A statistical question needs variability in its answers.
California has one capital, so everyone gives the same answer.
There is only one fact, so no, it is not statistical.
6.SP-8#0: With an even number of values, the median is the average of the two middle ones.
The set has 4 values in order; the middle two are 3 and 7.
Average the two middle values to find the halfway point: (3 + 7) ÷ 2 = 5.
The median of the set is 5.
6.SP-8#1: The mean is the sum of the values divided by how many there are.
Add the values: 6 + 8 + 10 = 24, and there are 3 of them.
Divide the sum by the count: 24 ÷ 3 = 8, so the mean is 8.
6.SP-9#0: Each dot on a dot plot is one measurement.
Dots stacked above 3 are the measurements that equal 3.
There are 4 dots above 3, so 4 measurements equal 3.
6.SP-9#1: In a histogram, the height of a bar is a count.
The bar from 20–29 counts the values that fall in that range.
Its height is 8, so 8 values are in that range.
6.SP-10#0: To find a mean, add the values and divide by the count.
Find the sum: 2 + 4 + 6 + 8 = 20, and the set has 4 values.
Share the sum equally: 20 ÷ 4 = 5, so the mean is 5.
6.SP-10#1: The range is the max minus the min.
In this set the max is 11 and the min is 2.
Take the min away from the max: 11 − 2 = 9, so the range is 9.
